title: 22. Interview: At Least Once Delivery
summary: Interview Q&A for At Least Once Delivery — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 At Least Once Delivery interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What does "at-least-once delivery" guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
**Answer:** At-least-once delivery guarantees that each message will be delivered to the consumer one or more times — never zero times (no silent loss). It does not guarantee exactly-once: the consumer may see the same message multiple times if the broker redelivers due to a lost ack, a consumer crash, or a visibility-timeout expiry during processing. Specifically, at-least-once guarantees: (1) If the producer successfully sends and the broker accepts, the message will be delivered (assuming the consumer eventually consumes). (2) If the consumer crashes or fails to ack, the message will be redelivered. (3) If the broker crashes and replicates, the message survives (with replication). It does not guarantee: (1) No duplicates — redeliveries can cause the consumer to see the same message twice. (2) Ordering across failures — a redelivered message may arrive after later messages have already been processed. (3) Bounded delivery time — if the consumer is slow or down, delivery is delayed indefinitely (until retention expires). The architect's takeaway: at-least-once gives you reliability (no losses) but requires idempotent consumers to handle duplicates.
**Visual:**
```
guarantees:        1+ deliveries per message (no losses)
does NOT guarantee: exactly-once (duplicates possible)
                    ordering across failures
                    bounded delivery latency
```

### Q2. Why is "ack after processing" critical in at-least-once consumers?
**Answer:** The ack is the consumer's signal to the broker that the message has been processed successfully and can be removed. If the consumer acks before processing completes (e.g., on receive, or mid-processing), and then crashes before finishing, the broker has already removed the message — it is lost, defeating the entire purpose of at-least-once. The correct pattern is: receive the message, process it fully (including all side effects like DB writes, downstream calls), and only then send the ack. If the consumer crashes during processing, no ack is sent, and the broker redelivers the message to another consumer (or the same one after restart), which re-processes it — at-least-once is preserved. This is why manual ack mode is essential: in RabbitMQ, use `basic_ack` after processing; in SQS, call `DeleteMessage` after processing; in Kafka, commit the offset after processing. Auto-ack modes (e.g., RabbitMQ's auto-ack, Kafka's auto-commit) are dangerous for at-least-once because they ack before processing completes. The visibility timeout / lease must be set longer than the worst-case processing time, otherwise the broker will redeliver while the original consumer is still working, causing concurrent duplicate processing — also a form of "acking too late" effectively.
**Visual:**
```
BAD:  receive -> ack -> process (crash = LOST)
GOOD: receive -> process -> ack (crash = REDELIVERED)
```

### Q3. How does the visibility timeout (lease) work, and how do you set it?
**Answer:** The visibility timeout is the period during which a delivered message is invisible to other consumers, giving the original consumer exclusive time to process. SQS calls it "visibility timeout" (default 30s, max 12h); RabbitMQ uses "consumer prefetch" with ack timeouts; Kafka uses `max.poll.interval.ms`. When a consumer receives a message, the broker hides it from other consumers for the timeout duration. If the consumer acks within the timeout, the message is removed. If the consumer does not ack (crash, slow processing), the timeout expires and the message becomes visible again — redelivered to another consumer. Set the timeout to "expected processing time + safety margin": for a job that typically takes 5s but can occasionally take 20s, set 30-60s. Too short: the broker redelivers while the original consumer is still working, causing concurrent duplicate processing (wasted work, potential races). Too long: a crashed consumer holds the message for the full timeout before redelivery, delaying recovery. SQS supports extending mid-processing via `ChangeMessageVisibility` — a long-running consumer can extend the lease if it knows it will take longer. Kafka's `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5min) is similar: if the consumer does not poll within this window, it is considered dead and rebalanced. The rule: timeout > p99 processing time, with margin for GC pauses and downstream slowness.
**Visual:**
```
deliver msg (invisible for 30s)
  consumer processes (5s) -> ack -> removed
  consumer crashes -> 30s expires -> msg visible -> redeliver
  consumer slow (45s) -> 30s expires -> redeliver (BAD: concurrent dup)
fix: extend lease with ChangeMessageVisibility for slow jobs
```

### Q4. How does Kafka's at-least-once consumer work?
**Answer:** Kafka's consumer is at-least-once by default. The consumer reads messages from a partition in order, processes them, and periodically commits its current offset (the position in the partition it has processed up to). The broker retains all messages for the retention period (default 7 days), so even committed messages can be re-read by seeking backward. If the consumer crashes before committing its offset, on restart it resumes from the last committed offset — re-reading and re-processing any messages it had processed but not committed. This is the at-least-once behavior: messages between the last commit and the crash are processed twice. To minimize duplicates, commit frequently (e.g., after each batch), but not so frequently that commit overhead dominates. Kafka offers two commit modes: auto-commit (default, every 5s) is convenient but dangerous — it commits on a timer regardless of processing progress, so a crash can lose messages you thought were committed. Manual commit (after processing) is the safe pattern. The `enable.auto.commit=false` setting is essential for at-least-once. The `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5min) bounds the inactivity window — if processing takes longer than this, the consumer is kicked out of the group and rebalanced, causing redelivery. The `max.poll.records` bounds the batch size — smaller batches commit more frequently (fewer duplicates on crash) but with more overhead.
**Visual:**
```
partition: [m1][m2][m3][m4][m5]
                          ^ committed offset
consumer reads m4, m5, processes -> CRASH (before commit)
restart: resume from m4 -> re-process m4, m5 (at-least-once)
```

### Q5. How do you make an at-least-once consumer idempotent?
**Answer:** Idempotency means processing the same message multiple times has the same effect as processing it once. There are several patterns: (1) **Natural idempotency**: the side effect is inherently idempotent — e.g., `UPDATE users SET status='active' WHERE id=42` produces the same result whether run once or twice. No dedup needed. (2) **Idempotency key**: each message carries a unique key, and the consumer records it in a dedup table before processing; a redelivery finds the key and skips (covered in the exactly-once topic). (3) **Content-based dedup**: the consumer computes a hash of the message content and uses it as the dedup key — useful when the producer does not assign IDs. (4) **External idempotency**: for external side effects (e.g., Stripe charges), use the external system's idempotency-key support. The choice depends on the side effect: for DB-only side effects, an idempotency key in a UNIQUE column is sufficient; for external APIs, the external system's idempotency support is required; for naturally idempotent operations, no dedup is needed. The dedup table must be retained long enough to cover the redelivery window (typically 7-30 days). Monitoring the dedup hit rate (should be >99% for most pipelines — most messages are first-time, with a small percentage of redeliveries caught by dedup) is essential for verifying idempotency is working.
**Visual:**
```
naturally idempotent:  UPDATE ... WHERE id=X (no dedup needed)
idempotency key:       dedup table + UNIQUE constraint
content hash:          hash(payload) as dedup key
external:              Stripe's Idempotency-Key header
```

### Q6. What is the difference between at-least-once and at-most-once, and when do you choose each?
**Answer:** At-least-once delivers each message 1+ times (no losses, possible duplicates); at-most-once delivers each message 0 or 1 times (possible losses, no duplicates). The choice depends on the cost of duplicates vs. losses. Choose at-least-once when losing a message is unacceptable: payments, orders, audit logs, user actions, anything where loss means lost revenue or broken invariants. The cost is duplicate-handling complexity (idempotency). Choose at-most-once when duplicates are worse than losses or when the value of each message is low: metrics, logs, telemetry, fire-and-forget notifications — here the cost of dedup infrastructure outweighs the value of each message, and an occasional lost metric is acceptable. The technical difference is the ack: at-least-once acks after processing (so redelivery happens on failure); at-most-once acks before processing (or does not ack at all — fire-and-forget), so a crash loses the message. Most MQ systems default to at-least-once because it is the safer choice for most use cases; at-most-once is reserved for special cases (UDP-based protocols, in-memory queues, low-value telemetry). The architect's rule: default to at-least-once; only downgrade to at-most-once when you have explicitly justified that losses are tolerable and dedup is too expensive.
**Visual:**
```
at-least-once: ack-after-process, redeliver on fail (no losses, dups)
at-most-once:  ack-before-process, no redeliver (losses, no dups)
choose at-least-once: payments, orders, audit (loss = bad)
choose at-most-once: metrics, logs, telemetry (loss = OK)
```

### Q7. What real-world systems use at-least-once delivery?
**Answer:** The vast majority of production message-queueing systems default to at-least-once. AWS SQS is at-least-once with a configurable visibility timeout and `ApproximateReceiveCount` for duplicate detection — it is the backbone of Amazon's order processing and countless AWS customer pipelines. Apache Kafka's default consumer is at-least-once (commit offset after processing); exactly-once is opt-in via transactions. RabbitMQ with manual acks is at-least-once — used by Instagram, Pinterest, and many traditional enterprises. Google Pub/Sub is at-least-once with an ack deadline (exactly-once delivery was added in 2023 for some configurations). ActiveMQ, IBM MQ, and Azure Service Bus all default to at-least-once. Real-world pipelines running on these: Netflix's event platform (Kafka at-least-once + idempotent consumers), Uber's trip pipeline (Kafka), Amazon's order pipeline (SQS), Stripe's webhook delivery (at-least-once with idempotency keys for merchants), and Slack's message delivery (Kafka + Redis). The pattern across all of these: the broker provides at-least-once, the consumer provides idempotency, and the system achieves effectively-exactly-once at the application level. At-least-once is so dominant because the alternative (at-most-once) silently loses data, which is unacceptable for most business pipelines.
**Visual:**
```
SQS:        at-least-once (visibility timeout + ApproximateReceiveCount)
Kafka:      at-least-once default (exactly-once opt-in via transactions)
RabbitMQ:   at-least-once (manual ack mode)
Pub/Sub:    at-least-once (ack deadline)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your SQS consumer receives a message, processes it (5 seconds), but the visibility timeout is 3 seconds. What happens?
**Answer:** The visibility timeout (3s) is shorter than the processing time (5s), so the broker will redeliver the message after 3 seconds — while the original consumer is still processing. Another consumer instance will receive the same message and start processing it concurrently. Now you have two consumers processing the same message, which can cause: (1) duplicate side effects (e.g., double-charging a customer if the consumer is not idempotent), (2) wasted work (both consumers do the same job), (3) race conditions on shared state. The original consumer will eventually finish and ack, but the redelivered copy may already have been processed. Fix: set the visibility timeout to "expected processing time + safety margin" — for a 5-second job, use 30-60 seconds to cover GC pauses and downstream slowness. SQS allows up to 12 hours. For jobs with highly variable processing time, use `ChangeMessageVisibility` to extend the timeout mid-processing — the consumer periodically extends the lease (e.g., every 10 seconds) until it finishes or fails. Without this fix, the consumer will see roughly 2x redelivery rate, and any non-idempotent side effects will be duplicated. Audit the consumer's idempotency as a defense-in-depth — even with correct timeouts, redeliveries can happen on consumer crashes.
**Visual:**
```
T=0s   deliver to A (invisible 3s)
T=3s   lease expires, redeliver to B (concurrent dup!)
T=5s   A finishes, acks; B also finishes, acks (or fails)
fix:   visibility_timeout = 30s (cover 5s + margin)
       OR extend lease via ChangeMessageVisibility
```

### Q2. Your Kafka consumer processes a batch of 500 messages and commits the offset. A crash occurs after processing 300 but before committing. What happens?
**Answer:** The consumer processed 300 messages but did not commit the offset, so on restart it resumes from the last committed offset — re-reading and re-processing all 500 messages, including the 300 that were already processed. This is the at-least-once behavior: the 300 messages are processed twice (once before the crash, once after). The architect's job is to ensure the consumer is idempotent so this re-processing does not cause duplicate side effects. The trade-off is between commit frequency and duplicate window: committing after every message minimizes the duplicate window (1 message re-processed on crash) but adds commit overhead; committing after every 500 messages minimizes overhead but re-processes up to 500 on crash. A common compromise is to commit after every batch (50-500 messages) — the duplicate window is bounded, the overhead is amortized. For non-idempotent side effects, use a per-message idempotency key in a dedup table so re-processing is a no-op. Kafka's `enable.auto.commit=false` is essential for explicit commit control; auto-commit (every 5s) commits on a timer regardless of processing progress, which can lose messages you thought were committed (if the consumer crashes after auto-commit but before processing). The rule: commit after processing, with a frequency that balances overhead and duplicate window, and always use idempotent consumers.
**Visual:**
```
batch: [m1..m500]
processed m1..m300 -> CRASH (no commit)
restart: resume from m1 -> re-process m1..m500 (at-least-once)
fix: idempotent consumer (dedup table)
     or commit more frequently (smaller duplicate window)
```

### Q3. Your order-processing pipeline uses SQS with at-least-once delivery. A customer reports being charged twice for the same order. How do you diagnose and fix?
**Answer:** Diagnose: (1) Check `ApproximateReceiveCount` on the SQS message — if it is >1, the message was redelivered, and the consumer processed it twice. (2) Check the consumer logs for the order ID — were there two processing events with the same order ID? (3) Check whether the consumer is idempotent — does it have a dedup table with the order ID as the key? If not, that is the root cause: at-least-once delivery + non-idempotent consumer = duplicates. (4) Check the visibility timeout — was it shorter than processing time, causing concurrent duplicate processing? Fix: (1) Add a dedup table with `order_id` as the UNIQUE key; in the consumer's DB transaction, check the dedup table first (skip if found), then apply the side effect (charge) and insert the dedup key, all atomically. (2) Refund the customer for the duplicate charge. (3) Set the visibility timeout to cover worst-case processing time. (4) Add monitoring on the dedup hit rate — if it is low (most keys not found), duplicates are slipping through; if it is high (most keys found), redeliveries are frequent and you may have a visibility-timeout or consumer-crash problem. (5) Add a DLQ for poison messages that would otherwise be infinitely redelivered. The root cause is almost always a missing or buggy idempotency layer; the broker is doing its job (at-least-once), and the consumer must handle duplicates.
**Visual:**
```
diagnose: ApproximateReceiveCount > 1?
          consumer logs show 2x processing?
          dedup table present and keyed on order_id?
fix:      dedup table + UNIQUE(order_id) + same-txn as charge
          refund customer, set visibility_timeout > p99 processing
```

### Q4. You need to deliver messages with strict ordering (per user) and at-least-once. How do you design this?
**Answer:** Use Kafka with the user ID as the partition key — all messages for a given user go to the same partition, and Kafka delivers them in order within the partition. A single consumer per partition processes them in order, ensuring per-user ordering. At-least-once is preserved: if the consumer crashes, the broker redelivers from the last committed offset, and the consumer re-processes in order. The key considerations: (1) Partition by the entity you need ordering for (user, order, etc.) — different entities can be on different partitions and processed in parallel. (2) Use a single consumer per partition (no concurrency within a partition) — if you scale out, you scale partitions, not consumers-per-partition. (3) Commit the offset only after processing, to maintain at-least-once. (4) Be aware that a poison message (one that always fails) blocks the partition — all subsequent messages for that user are stuck behind it. Use a DLQ to sideline poison messages and unblock the partition. (5) On a partition rebalance (consumer joins/leaves), ordering is preserved within each partition but processing may pause briefly during rebalance. SQS FIFO queues also provide per-message-group ordering with at-least-once, but with lower throughput than Kafka. The architect's rule: partition by ordering key, single consumer per partition, commit after processing, DLQ for poison messages.
**Visual:**
```
producer: send(user_id=42, msg) -> hash(42) % N = partition 3
partition 3: [m1@u42][m2@u42][m3@u42]  (in order)
consumer A (partition 3): process m1, m2, m3 in order
crash after m2 (no commit) -> restart from m1 -> re-process in order
```

### Q5. Your consumer takes 2 minutes to process each message (heavy compute). The SQS visibility timeout max is 12 hours. How do you handle this without concurrent duplicates?
**Answer:** Use `ChangeMessageVisibility` to extend the lease mid-processing. The consumer receives the message with an initial visibility timeout (e.g., 60 seconds), then periodically (e.g., every 30 seconds) calls `ChangeMessageVisibility` to reset the timeout back to 60 seconds, as long as it is still processing. This keeps the message invisible to other consumers throughout the 2-minute processing window. If the consumer crashes, the extensions stop, and after the last-set timeout expires, the message becomes visible and is redelivered — at-least-once is preserved. Alternative patterns: (1) Decouple the heavy processing from the queue consumer — the consumer receives the message, enqueues the work to a background job system (e.g., a worker pool), and acks immediately. The worker system handles its own retries and at-least-once semantics. This is the recommended pattern for long-running jobs because it frees the consumer thread quickly. (2) Use a step-function or workflow engine (AWS Step Functions, Temporal) that manages the long-running job state and retries. (3) Split the work into smaller chunks (each <60 seconds) and process them as separate messages, so each fits within a normal visibility timeout. The choice depends on the workload: for inherently long jobs, the background-worker decoupling is cleanest; for splittable work, chunking is most efficient.
**Visual:**
```
T=0s    receive (visibility=60s), start processing
T=30s   ChangeMessageVisibility(60s) -> expires at T=90s
T=60s   ChangeMessageVisibility(60s) -> expires at T=120s
T=90s   ChangeMessageVisibility(60s) -> expires at T=150s
T=120s  finish processing, ack
crash at T=100s: no more extensions -> expires at T=150s -> redeliver
```

### Q6. You are migrating from at-most-once (fire-and-forget UDP) to at-least-once (Kafka) for telemetry. What changes?
**Answer:** The migration involves several changes: (1) **Producer**: switch from UDP send-to-broker to Kafka producer with `acks=all` (wait for all in-sync replicas) and retries enabled — this guarantees the message reaches the broker durably. The producer's latency increases (from microseconds for UDP to single-digit milliseconds for Kafka with acks). (2) **Consumer**: switch from passive UDP listener to Kafka consumer with manual offset commit (after processing) — this enables at-least-once redelivery. (3) **Idempotency**: telemetry was previously non-idempotent (a duplicate metric would inflate counts); now you need to handle duplicates, e.g., by using timestamped metrics that dedup naturally, or by accepting duplicates as noise for aggregation purposes. (4) **Visibility timeout / max.poll.interval.ms**: set appropriately for the consumer's processing time. (5) **DLQ**: add a DLQ for poison messages that cannot be processed (e.g., malformed telemetry). (6) **Monitoring**: track consumer lag, redelivery rate, and DLQ depth. (7) **Cost**: Kafka is significantly more expensive than UDP (storage, replication, broker compute) — justify the cost by the value of not losing telemetry. (8) **Latency**: Kafka adds latency vs. UDP, which may matter for real-time alerting. The trade-off is reliability (no losses) vs. cost/latency — for most business-critical telemetry, the trade-off favors Kafka; for high-volume low-value telemetry (per-request traces), at-most-once may still be appropriate.
**Visual:**
```
before (UDP):  send -> broker -> consumer (fire-and-forget, losses OK)
after (Kafka): send (acks=all) -> broker (durable) -> consumer (commit)
               + idempotency (or accept dups for aggregations)
               + DLQ for poison msgs
               + monitoring (lag, redelivery, DLQ depth)
```

### Q7. Your at-least-once consumer's dedup table is hitting the DB hard (a SELECT per message). How do you scale?
**Answer:** The per-message dedup lookup is a common bottleneck for high-volume at-least-once consumers. Several scaling options: (1) **Cache the dedup keys in Redis**: check Redis first (sub-millisecond), fall back to DB on miss, and write-through to both. This handles 100k+ QPS per Redis instance. (2) **Batch the dedup lookups**: instead of one SELECT per message, batch 100 messages and do a single `SELECT key FROM dedup WHERE key IN (...)`. This amortizes the round-trip and works for moderate volumes. (3) **Use a Bloom filter**: a probabilistic data structure that can quickly say "definitely not in dedup" or "maybe in dedup" — for the "maybe" case, fall back to the DB. Bloom filters fit in memory and handle millions of keys with low false-positive rate. (4) **Use Kafka transactions / exactly-once**: if the side effect is to another Kafka topic, you can use transactions to avoid the dedup table entirely (Kafka dedups internally). (5) **Partition the dedup table**: shard by key hash so lookups distribute across DB shards. (6) **Use a content-addressable store**: for content-hash keys, a KV store like DynamoDB or Cassandra with single-digit-millisecond lookups at scale. The right choice depends on volume and latency requirements: for <10k QPS, a DB with batching is fine; for 100k+ QPS, Redis or a Bloom filter is typical. Always monitor the dedup hit rate and lookup latency as part of the consumer's SLO.
**Visual:**
```
per-message SELECT:  ~1ms * 100k QPS = 100 cores of DB (too much)
fix: Redis cache (sub-ms), batch IN-clause, Bloom filter, or
     partition the dedup table, or use Kafka transactions
```
